C’est aujourd’hui que se tiennent les fu: The funeral of Haiti’s former president, Jovenel Moïse, is being held today in Cap-Haïtien, near his home region. Early in the morning last July 7, the President of the Republic of Haiti was assassinated by an armed commando at his private residence in Port-au-Prince, the country’s capital. First Lady Martine Moïse has returned to the country after being treated in a Miami hospital.
Qu’est-ce qui a mené à cet événement? Re: What led to this event? A look at a neglected context.
Née au Québec, l’intervenante psychosoci: Born in Quebec, psychosocial worker Josiane Ménard speaks of vicarious trauma: “These aren’t things that happen to you directly, but you live them anyway,” she explains. She fears that, without context, people will paint a grim picture of the country. “I had to defend my country. In the middle of mourning, we also have to respond to aggressions and micro-aggressions,” she confided to us on the day of the assassination.
Mme Ménard n’a pas encore eu l’occasion: Ms. Ménard has not yet had the chance to visit her country of origin, and hopes to hold her cousins and their children in her arms. “It’s one of my dearest dreams. It would be too great a loss to close the door and never go,” she laments. She hopes that the world’s first independent Black republic will find stability.
<strong>Le périple d’un ancien fonctionn: The journey of a former civil servant
C’est une aspiration à laquelle <em>Jona: It’s an aspiration that Jonas* echoes. Seated at a table in the Place Versailles food court, he tells us about his journey. Unlike Ms. Ménard, Jonas was born in Haiti and lived there almost all his life. After working for the Haitian federal government for more than 15 years, he is afraid to go back. Under the presidency of Jovenel Moïse, the civil servant was threatened and assaulted. “I had two choices: either I stay to keep fighting, but if I stayed, death was there too,” he says sadly. A refugee in Quebec since March 2020, he is deeply troubled by the head of state’s assassination. His wife and two children are still in Haiti. “It’s a fragile country, we don’t know what will happen tomorrow and the day after,” he says.
Jonas a travaillé pour un parti de l’opp: Jonas worked for an opposition party before working in the office of Haiti’s Minister of Public Health. In the course of his duties, he met former president Jovenel Moïse several times. He saw in him goodwill, but a poor candidate to lead the Republic. “What I noticed is that he was a novice politician. He was someone with good intentions, but who didn’t really know what he was doing, where to start, or what means to use to achieve his ends,” he recalls. A few years later, Jonas landed a position at the Office d’assurance accidents du travail maladie et maternité (OFATMA).
Il y observe de près la fraude qui a lie: There, he closely observed the fraud taking place under the Moïse administration. “I discovered large-scale corruption involving not only OFATMA’s director general, but also the First Lady and many other prominent figures in the country,” says the former civil servant. In 2018, he noticed that all of the funds of the OFATMA Hospital in Port-au-Prince had disappeared. The facility’s former director, Hans Herbert Boucher, left his position leaving accounts emptied of 16 million gourdes, or more than $216,000 Canadian.
« Dans l’intervalle de deux semaines, to: “Within two weeks, everything had disappeared. Nothing was bought for the hospital. Nothing was paid toward debts, and we found no documents showing that the hospital had debts,” explains Jonas. Jonas and his colleagues reported it to OFATMA’s director general, Agabus Joseph. They were met with threats, had sanctions imposed on them, and faced transfers and dismissals. Jonas and his colleagues then decided to make the matter public and sent a letter to institutions able to conduct investigations, including President Jovenel Moïse. But the letter did not have the desired effect. After a meeting with the president during a parliamentary session, Agabus Joseph transferred Jonas to Port-de-Paix, a municipality in the northeast of the country located 165 km from the capital. Those around him are adamant: they believe it was a plot to kill him. The threats became real during a general assembly held in a hospital.
« J’ai été agressé et battu. Ses hommes: “I was attacked and beaten. His men pointed a gun at me,” says Jonas, who notes that the police did not intervene when he and his colleagues called for help. After this assault, Jonas and his wife, who was pregnant at the time, lived in uncertainty. They left the city, fearing they would be killed. Finally, in 2020, the former civil servant left the country. He crossed the continent to land in Montréal. He is waiting to be able to bring his wife and two children here. Jonas considers a return to Haiti dangerous, even impossible, for him. The political refugee believes the president’s assassination was organized by foreign forces, with the collaboration of people close to Jovenel Moïse. Following our conversation, he worries about his family.
Frantz André œuvre auprès du Comité d’ac: Frantz André works with the Comité d’action des personnes sans statut (CAPSS). He supports several Haitian refugees every day. While some of them apply for economic reasons, the community worker believes the reasons for their exile are more complex. “Economic refugees often leave the country for political reasons,” Mr. André states right away. Among these nationals are former civil servants, police officers, judges and lawyers who, like Jonas, were threatened by the government. The economic reasons cited thus often stem from the fact that these refugees can no longer practise their profession or hold a job, on top of fearing for their safety. “Many migration problems are linked to these lack of opportunities, caused by politics. The two shouldn’t be separated,” explains the social worker. He says politics is also used as a tool to settle personal problems, for example by denouncing someone with whom one has some kind of dispute. The political asylum claim is a laborious process. “Haiti is not a place where it is easy to justify political reasons.
Les gens partent souvent à la sauvette,: People often leave in a hurry, they often don’t have time to prepare files with evidence,” explains the activist. His task is therefore to gather evidence to support asylum claim statements, by doing research. Claims often rely on testimonies, which can be challenged by the commissioner at the hearing, for lack of documented evidence. However, even authenticating documents from Haiti can be arduous, and Mr. André describes the difficulty of getting immigration authorities to understand that they are legitimate. While Frantz André dares to expose himself despite the threats he receives, the president’s assassination plunges Haitian refugees even further into fear. “These asylum seekers probably don’t want to say too much, for fear that their families will be affected,” he says. “In the current situation, if there is one intervention the international community can make, including Canada, it’s to secure these people and bring their families here,” he concludes.
Frantz Voltaire, historien, politologue: Frantz Voltaire, historian, political scientist and director of the Centre international de documentation et d’information haïtienne, caribéenne et afro-canadienne (CIDIHCA), describes the political, economic and social climate in Haiti in which the president’s assassination occurred. In their new office in Old Montréal, surrounded by books and numerous archives on Haiti, the historian explains that the country has been doing poorly since the 2010 earthquake. He believes that at the time, instead of putting solid institutions in place, the Clinton Foundation, and the intervention of Bill Clinton himself, favoured the hasty organization of elections, which were held in 2011. The term of President Michel Martelly, in office from 2011 to 2016, is said to have worsened the situation. “The election of Michel Martelly was facilitated, and afterward, that of Jovenel Moïse was just as readily facilitated under the same conditions, after the Petrocaribe crisis caused by a massive embezzlement of funds under the Martelly administration,” he points out. The fruit-production company Agritrans, which belongs to Jovenel Moïse, is accused of having misappropriated substantial funds even before its owner’s presidency.
« On parle de 30 millions de dollars can: “We’re talking about 30 million Canadian dollars that were meant to relaunch Haitian agriculture. All of it was a scam and there was no follow-up to this project,” explains Mr. Voltaire. These funds came from Petrocaribe, through which Venezuela sold subsidized oil to Haiti. The State was supposed to use the proceeds to finance social and infrastructure projects, to build hospitals and roads. The political scientist says he understands the anger of the Haitian people, who face loans they will have to repay but that were mismanaged, “and in the worst cases embezzled for the benefit of a political and economic elite,” he adds. Protests have not stopped proliferating across the country demanding Jovenel Moïse’s departure; he was accused of being mixed up in corruption and of financing armed gangs.
Certains de ces gangs proclamaient ouver: Some of these gangs openly claimed to support Jovenel Moïse. These heavily armed gangs that terrorize the population are a problem that has affected Haiti for some time. The Jovenel Moïse administration was unable to stem this violence. “Weapons and ammunition could be controlled upstream,” says Mr. Voltaire, adding that an agreement should be reached with American police authorities to limit and control the boats that enter Haitian territory and feed the clandestine channels of the country’s ports.
Hormis ses échecs dans les finances et l: Aside from his failures in finance and public safety, President Jovenel Moïse also faced other major difficulties during his term. At the scheduled end of the presidential term, on February 7, 2021, elections had still not been held, because the outgoing parliament refused to approve the electoral law, which must nevertheless be ratified for each election. Without a parliament, the former president governed by decree, meaning that he issued orders to carry out the State’s decisions. His decisions therefore could not be challenged. As a result, the country plunged into economic and political disorder, on top of grappling with armed gang violence in working-class neighbourhoods. Several decisions were denounced by the opposition and the public, notably the decision to hold a referendum to reshape the constitution.
Le vote, prévu le 26 juin dernier, a été: The vote, scheduled for June 26, was postponed because of the health crisis. By amending the constitution, Jovenel Moïse planned, among other things, to grant the right to vote to the Haitian diaspora, which represents roughly more than three million people and 40% of the country’s GDP. He opposed the installation of a transitional government, arguing that it would avoid a waste of resources, time, money and personnel. Frantz Voltaire, however, considers this “cheap rhetoric.” For his part, the former president denounced a Haitian oligarchy made up of large private-sector companies that sign overbilled contracts with the State.
Elles bénéficient de notes de crédit qui: They benefit from credit notes that allow them to be paid directly by the Banque de la République d’Haïti in case of delay. The institution is responsible for regulating the Haitian banking system and releases funds from the public treasury. This scheme is estimated at about 10 million Canadian dollars every month. “I think the president, through his arbitrary authoritarian management, had an enormous number of enemies. When you have all these enemies, it’s a little harder to understand who might have an interest in this assassination,” explains Mr. Voltaire.
Le 12 juillet dernier, Marie Dimanche or: On July 12, Marie Dimanche organized a vigil in solidarity with the Haitian people, shaken by the assassination, in front of the Consulate General of Haiti in Montréal. While several people present said they feared for their loved ones and dreaded the outbreak of a civil war, another event this week at the Haitian cultural association La Perle retrouvée instead paid tribute to the president whom Jonas and so many other refugees fled, with doves released into the sky in his memory. Two perspectives, one reality in which uncertainty reigns for the Haitian people and the diaspora. In the meantime, the investigation into the former president’s assassination remains ongoing, even though many doubt the truth will ever come to light.
La loi électorale haïtienne doit être ap: Haiti’s electoral law must be approved at the end of each term by the sitting government. It creates the Provisional Electoral Council, which is responsible for organizing presidential elections. Under the constitution amended in 1987, at the end of the Duvalier dictatorship, the president alone does not have the authority required to organize elections.
Puisque les élections législatives n’ont: Because legislative elections were not held, the Senate was rendered inoperative. The terms of most of the sitting senators ended on January 13, 2020. Ten senators, who had been elected to longer terms, remain in office. The Senate must have 15 members to have a quorum.
Jovenel Moïse, de même que son successeu: Jovenel Moïse, like his interim successor Ariel Henry, enjoyed the support of the international community through the Core Group. The Core Group was set up in 2004 with the deployment of troops to forcibly escort the then-president, Jean-Bertrand Aristide. It is made up of the ambassadors of Germany, Brazil, Canada, Spain, the United States, France and the European Union, as well as the Special Representative of the Organization of American States and the Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General. To this day, little information exists on the role and workings of this entity.
Le Core Group a accepté la continuité du: The Core Group accepted the continuation of the presidential term even after February 7, 2021, the scheduled end date of his mandate, even though this extension of the term violated the Haitian constitution. Political scientist Frantz Voltaire considers the Core Group to be the body that steers Haitian politics. He hopes that parliamentary, fiscal and judicial reforms will be put in place and, above all, that a transparent permanent electoral council will be created in the coming months. “I believe these reforms are necessary if we want to open the country to modernity, if we want to resolve a good part of the social inequalities that exist in this country,” he says.
